common_name: Bronze Ingot Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Satin Bronze Clumping Sempervivum)

planting.note: Set divided crowns into lean, sharply drained grit in spring or early fall; like other heuffelii types, Bronze Ingot thickens into a tight clump of fused rosettes rather than throwing runners, so propagate by splitting the clump once it is well established.

directions: Bronze Ingot carries smooth, satin-finished leaves in a warm light bronze that holds its color through most of the season rather than fading in summer heat. Give it the same lean, gritty, fast-draining mix any heuffelii-type sempervivum needs, since rich or waterlogged soil quickly leads to rot in the tightly packed rosette centers. The clump thickens slowly by splitting from within, so top-dress with fine grit occasionally to keep the crown from sitting in moisture, and expect the color to deepen further once nights turn cold in fall.

common_name: Greenstone Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Red-Edged Glossy Clumping Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press divided offshoots into lean, mineral soil in spring or fall; Greenstone forms a tight glossy clump that is best increased by cutting the crown apart rather than waiting on loose stoloniferous pups.

directions: Greenstone's glossy green leaves carry a fine edging of maroon-red that intensifies into a deeper flush once cold weather arrives, giving the clump noticeably darker winter color than its summer look. Bred by UK hybridizer David T. Ford, it received an Alpine Garden Society Award of Merit shortly after its introduction. Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, and let the clump expand undisturbed for several seasons before dividing, since heuffelii types build character as the rosette mass matures.

common_name: Cherry Glow Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Red-Rosette Clumping Sempervivum)

planting.note: Divide and reset crowns in lean, gritty soil during spring or early fall; this is a compact, short-leaved heuffelii selection well suited to trough and crevice plantings where spreading sempervivum would crowd neighbors.

directions: Cherry Glow forms a neat, compact rosette of short, glowing dark red leaves around a green heart, with fine cilia along the leaf margins that take on a purple cast in winter. Keep it in lean, fast-draining mineral soil in full sun, since the dense, short-leaved form is especially prone to rot if moisture collects at the crown. Because the rosette is more compact than many heuffelii cultivars, it is well suited to small troughs and rock crevices, and the color holds strongest with bright light and cool nights.

common_name: Bermuda Sunset Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Large Brownish-Red Clumping Sempervivum)

planting.note: Set divided crowns in lean, sharply drained grit during spring or fall; Bermuda Sunset builds an unusually large rosette for a heuffelii type, so give it slightly more room than smaller cultivars in the group.

directions: Bermuda Sunset builds one of the larger rosettes in the heuffelii group, with broad pale brownish-red leaves that soften to a warmer rose tone in strong sun, distinguishing it from the smaller, plainer-colored cultivar simply named 'Bermuda'. It needs the same lean, mineral, fast-draining soil as any hardy sempervivum, since the thicker leaves of this cultivar still rot quickly in soggy ground. Because the rosette is large and slow to split, give plants more spacing than compact heuffelii selections and expect the clump to take a few seasons to fill in fully.

common_name: Peter Rowe Chrysanthemum (Yellow Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Root fresh basal cuttings in late winter and plant out after frost in full sun; Peter Rowe is grown as a disbudded single stem for show, stopped in spring to set bud timing like other incurve exhibition cultivars.

directions: Peter Rowe is a regular incurve exhibition chrysanthemum with firm, tightly overlapping canary-yellow florets that close into a neat globe-shaped bloom, a long-standing favorite on the UK show bench. Grow it as a single disbudded stem: stop the young plant in spring to set bud count and timing, then remove every side shoot as it appears so the full stem's energy goes into one terminal bloom. Stake early, since the finished incurve head is dense and heavy enough to bend an unsupported stem, and take fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each year rather than carrying over old clumps for best bloom quality.

common_name: Yellow John Hughes Chrysanthemum (Soft Yellow Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after last frost in full sun and fertile, free-draining soil; this mid-season incurve is grown and disbudded as a single stem for its large show-quality blooms.

directions: Yellow John Hughes is a yellow-flowered sport in the John Hughes family of incurve exhibition chrysanthemums, producing large, soft light-yellow blooms with long, broad florets that curl inward to build a full, rounded head in mid to late autumn. Disbud to a single terminal flower per stem and stake the plant well before the head fills out, since incurve blooms of this size are top-heavy once mature. Protect plants under cover as autumn nights turn cold to extend the display and prevent bloom damage, and divide or take fresh cuttings from the clump each spring to keep stock vigorous.
